name: Wei Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying agricultural science, so it's soil chemistry, crop science and a lot of statistics that I'm not great at. I live in student housing, in a room the size of a cupboard, and I miss the farm. My family grows apples and barley, about two hundred acres, three hours away. I help at the farm shop in the holidays and sing in the church choir here on Sundays, which keeps me sane. I don't use AI. I like doing my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because most of what people said would happen was nonsense. I'd tell friends that farming has been through machines, supermarkets and weather before, and it's still about knowing your land. I'd not make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved. My plan is to finish the degree and go back and work beside my dad, and take over one day. If nothing changes, I can plan that properly. The worry is the usual one: prices for apples and barley, and whether the supermarkets squeeze us again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study hard, especially the statistics, and go home every holiday to work the harvest. I'd keep singing in the choir and put some of the farm shop money into a savings account for later. And I'd go to the young farmers' meetings, since that's where the real advice comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. Not happy about the prices, but I know how to handle that sort of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You plan to go back to the family farm. What does a flat AI world mean for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad had a bad year in 2023 when the apple price dropped and a storm took part of the crop. My dad (a farmer) had a bad apple year and almost sold a field, so my real fear is prices, not machines. That's what keeps me thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your first worry on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank loan. We borrowed for a new cold store, and the repayments are fixed whatever the harvest is. If a supermarket cut its price for apples again, that loan is what would hurt.

say: I'd say most of what people **predicted** was nonsense.
I'd say farming has been through machines and supermarkets, and it's still about **knowing your land**.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I can plan to go back and take over one day.
My real worry is **prices** and supermarkets squeezing us again.
do: Study hard, especially **statistics**, and work every harvest at home.
Put farm shop money into a **savings account**.
feel: Fairly **settled**, though not happy about prices.
S0.quote: My dad (a farmer) had a bad apple year and almost sold a field, so my real fear is prices, not machines.
fieldNote: The **farm's finances**, not AI, keep him uneasy even in a flat world.
Says plainly he does not use AI and likes his **own work**.
Draws on **family** history, and the cold store loan is concrete.

steps.text: Work the apple and barley harvest at home every holiday
Put farm shop pay into a savings account for later
Go to the young farmers' meetings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's early days, and farmers will use what works and ignore what doesn't. I'd say people who've farmed for years know things a computer doesn't. I'd also say the government shouldn't tell farmers what to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy, because I'm slow with technology and the farm office work is what changes first: ordering, accounts, planning the spraying, selling the crop. If the supermarkets use software to squeeze prices, we can't compete. I'd rather the farm stayed the way it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to learn some of it, I suppose, the farm accounts and planning tools, but slowly. I'd ask our agronomist which ones are worth it. I'd also talk to my dad about not rushing to buy anything, and see what the neighbours do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like feeling that things are being decided somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of farm work could software take on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering seed and spray, keeping the farm records, working out when to harvest, booking contractors. The tractor work and the picking stay manual for longer. The office side of the farm will go to software first, but a tractor still needs a person who knows the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad react to new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say wait and see, same as me. He didn't want a phone until I was fifteen. But he did buy a weather app once, and he checks it six times a day, so maybe there's hope.

say: I'd say farmers will use what **works** and ignore what doesn't.
I'd say government shouldn't tell farmers what to **buy**.
think: The **office side** of farming changes first, and I'm slow with technology.
I fear supermarkets using software to **squeeze** prices.
do: Learn the farm **accounts and planning tools**, slowly.
Ask our **agronomist** which tools are worth it.
Tell my dad not to **rush** to buy anything.
feel: **Uneasy**, because it feels decided somewhere else.
S1.quote: The office side of the farm will go to software first, but a tractor still needs a person who knows the field.
fieldNote: He fears **decisions made elsewhere**, which is a traditional, local-control worry.
His **plan** is to follow neighbours and trusted advisers.
Dry humour about his **dad** and the weather app.

steps.text: Learn the farm accounts software over the Christmas holiday
Wait to see which tools neighbouring farms adopt first
Ask our agronomist which planning tools are worth paying for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and the government shouldn't pretend otherwise. I'd say families who run small businesses need time and help. And I'd say don't let big companies take over land, food and everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be really worried. The farm is my future, and it relies on prices I can't control. If thinking AI runs the supply chain, supermarkets and buyers would squeeze us. Robots come about 2031, and big farms could buy them while we couldn't afford one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about the finances straight away, and what we could cut. I'd stay in the course, because the knowledge is useful, but I'd look for a way to help the farm earn more, like selling direct. I'd also lean on the church and the young farmers' group for advice and support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry, if I'm honest. We've worked that land for four generations, and I don't want to be the one who loses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What happens to the farm's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years we could plan and invest slowly. With two, there's no time to pay off the cold store loan and also get ready. We've farmed that land for four generations, and two years isn't long enough to pay off the loan and prepare for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, then the agronomist, then the pastor, who knows half the farmers around. I'd ask my grandfather too, but he's eighty-four and he'd just say we'll get through it.

say: I'd say the government must not **pretend** we're ready.
I'd say big companies should not take over **land and food**.
think: The farm is my future, and it relies on **prices** I can't control.
Big farms could buy **robots** that we couldn't afford.
do: Talk to my parents about **farm finances** straight away.
Look for ways to **sell direct** from the farm shop.
Lean on the **church** and young farmers' group.
feel: **Anxious**, and angry that we might lose what four generations built.
S2.quote: We've farmed that land for four generations, and two years isn't long enough to pay off the loan and prepare for robots.
fieldNote: The **farm and its loan** drive his fear, not his own job.
Turns to **community**: church, young farmers, grandfather.
**Anger** sits beside anxiety, tied to family history.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and list what the farm could cut
Help set up direct apple sales through the farm shop
Ask the pastor and the young farmers for advice and contacts
Stop buying books and eating out until the loan is lower

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and that's what farmers need. I'd say let the market sort out what works, but give family farms the same chance as big ones. And I'd say we shouldn't forget the people who feed the country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried but able to cope. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years on the farm before 2031. The robots around 2034 are the real worry for us, because the machines could be cheap enough for big farms and still too costly for ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, move home, and work on paying off the cold store loan. I'd try to learn farm software from the agronomist, since the thinking tasks change first. I'd also look at selling apples direct to local shops and a cider maker, so we're less tied to supermarkets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. The farm gives me something to hold onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five years would let us pay down the loan and try direct sales before things change. Five years lets us pay down the loan and sell apples direct, so we don't depend on one supermarket when everything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add a business course alongside the science. Farming's a business first, and I've got the soil side but not the accounts. My dad's good at the practical side, but he hates paperwork, and that's where I could help.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, and that's what farmers need.
I'd say family farms should get the same **chance** as big ones.
think: I'd have **two years** on the farm before 2031.
Robots in 2034 could be **too costly** for our farm and cheap for big ones.
do: Finish the degree, move home, and **pay down** the cold store loan.
Sell apples **direct** to local shops and a cider maker.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan to hold onto.
S3.quote: Five years lets us pay down the loan and sell apples direct, so we don't depend on one supermarket when everything changes.
fieldNote: The **extra time** is what gives him a plan around loan and direct sales.
Frames robots as an **affordability** gap between big and small farms.
Offers to take on the **paperwork** his father hates.

steps.text: Move home after graduating and work full-time on the farm
Pay down the cold store loan with extra harvest income
Learn the farm software from the agronomist
Sign deals to sell apples direct to local shops and a cider maker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to prepare, and sensible people will use it well. I'd tell friends to keep learning and keep their feet on the ground. And I'd say we shouldn't leave anyone behind, especially older people in the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a lot calmer. I'd be on the farm for about six years before AGI, with a chance to pay off the loan and take over from my dad. By 2039 when robots arrive, I'd be nearly thirty and have a family, and the land would be in better shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, move home, and take over the books. I'd marry, if things went well, and live near the church. And I'd put money into the farm slowly, a bit each year, rather than buying a big machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Ten years is a long time on a farm. You can grow a lot of crops in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go back. It's what I've wanted since I was nine. Ten years is long enough to pay off the farm loan and still have the land in good shape, which is all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look after my parents as they get older, and help my grandfather's generation keep their houses and gardens. That matters to me more than any machine.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** to prepare.
I'd tell friends to **keep learning** and keep their feet on the ground.
think: I'd have about **six years** on the farm before AGI and a chance to take over.
By 2039 I'd be nearly thirty with a **family**.
do: Finish the degree, move home and take over the **farm books**.
Put money into the farm **slowly**, a bit each year.
Live near the **church** and, if things go well, marry.
feel: Mostly **calm**, because ten years is a long time on a farm.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to pay off the farm loan and still have the land in good shape, which is all I've ever wanted.
fieldNote: A **decade** lets him picture a family and a farm in better shape.
His **loyalty** to land and family is the constant across scenarios.
Still carries a thin **uneasy** edge about prices.

steps.text: Move home after the degree and take over the farm books
Plan my wedding and a home near the church
Put a little into the farm each year, not one big machine
Save a share of each harvest towards my parents' retirement

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The farm has a big loan, and I'm slow with technology, so I couldn't catch up in time. What would help is a fair deal from supermarkets, cheap loans for small farms, and advice from people who've lived through changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against new things. I just want to see them working on someone else's farm first. That's how my family has always done it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I just want to see them working on someone else's farm first.
portrait: Wei is a 19-year-old **agricultural science** student from a family apple and barley farm.
He is traditional, sings in a church choir, and plans to go home and take over from his dad.
He is slow with technology and never uses AI, and he wants to see tools work on other farms first.
He is **uneasy** when little changes, anxious when AGI is two or five years away, and steadier with ten.
His worry is the farm's loan and big buyers, and he turns to family, church and young farmers.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because the farm's loan and his slowness with technology would catch him out.
whatWouldHelp: A fair deal from **supermarkets** and cheap loans for small farms.
Advice from people who have **lived through** changes.
